name: Spiritual left
summary: The spiritual left grounds left-wing goals of peace, economic justice and ecological care in religious or spiritual traditions rather than secular ones. It holds that politics should be judged by love, generosity and awe rather than money and power alone, and it contests the religious right's claim to speak for faith. Its best-known voices are Rabbi Michael Lerner of Tikkun and Jim Wallis of Sojourners.
scope: The contemporary American religious and spiritual progressive current represented by Michael Lerner (Tikkun, the Network of Spiritual Progressives, the New Bottom Line and Spiritual Covenant) and Jim Wallis (Sojourners, God's Politics). It is interfaith and mostly liberal-democratic in method. It excludes secular left, theocratic and conservative religious politics, and many specific policy questions are unaddressed by these writers, so many answers are low-confidence inferences.

sources.author: Michael Lerner
sources.usedFor: The New Bottom Line, Global Marshall Plan, opposition to the Iraq war, two-state position and opposition to imposing a religion.

sources.title: Interview with Rabbi Michael Lerner
sources.author: Grist

sources.title: Love Thine Political Enemies: Reflections on God's Politics and the Teachings of Christ
sources.author: Reflections, Yale Divinity School
sources.usedFor: Wallis on poverty, budgets as moral documents, war, church and state, and faith in civil rights.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Lerner explicitly backs universal health care and adequate education for all as part of a higher standard of living.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Lerner wants institutions judged by a New Bottom Line of love and caring rather than money and efficiency, and rejects a globalization of selfishness.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Lerner attacks the religious right for cutting taxes for the rich while cutting programs for the poor.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Lerner's covenant would add a social responsibility requirement to corporate conduct and judge firms by the New Bottom Line.

cut-welfare.rationale: Lerner condemns cuts to social programs for the poor as a misuse of religion.

state-harmful.rationale: Lerner wants government to fund health, education and anti-poverty programs, so he does not view the state as harmful.

empower-police-military.rationale: Lerner rejects militarism and the Strategy of Domination and wants resources redirected to a Global Marshall Plan.

traditional-family.rationale: Wallis stresses family but liberal spiritual progressives reject the religious right's family politics; adherents are split.

more-religion-public.rationale: Wallis argues faith belongs in public debate and Lerner wants spiritual values brought into politics, while opposing imposing any one religion.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Lerner favors global cooperation through a Global Marshall Plan, but does not discuss the UN.

free-trade.rationale: Lerner contrasts a globalization of love and caring with the existing globalization of selfishness.

nation-first.rationale: Lerner's Global Marshall Plan has rich countries giving 1-2% of GDP annually to end global poverty, the opposite of putting national interests first.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Adherents prize both human rights and peace, and the sources only oppose Iraq and Iran strikes.

limit-growth.rationale: Lerner urges consuming less and rethinking what counts as progress.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Lerner says ecological sanity is central and that an ecological movement must be spiritual; no specific climate program cited.

land-value-tax.rationale: Land taxation is a technical fiscal device that none of the sources mention and that the movement's ethics do not decide.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: The sources oppose selfish globalization but also global solidarity, so inference is unclear.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Lerner wants institutions steered by love and caring, but neither source says the state should pick strategic industries.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Lerner's economic democracy and communal sharing point away from concentrated ownership, but the sources never endorse a distributist small-owner program.

one-party-rule.rationale: The network works by persuading legislators and the public, a pluralist method that excludes a single guiding party.

democracy-best.rationale: Lerner's covenant approach lobbies elected representatives, which presumes democracy, but neither source defends it against bad voter choices.

natural-rulers.rationale: Lerner's ethic of equal spiritual worth and opposition to domination rejects any natural ruling class.

war-builds-character.rationale: Lerner wants a Strategy of Generosity in place of domination and demands an end to the Iraq war, a view hostile to glorifying war.

separate-church-state.rationale: Wallis explicitly does not seek to erase the line yet wants faith voices in debate, and Lerner opposes imposing a religion, leaving adherents on both sides of strict separation.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Lerner opposes imposing one particular religion on everyone and criticizes the religious right's use of the Bible to justify policy.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Privatizing core public functions contradicts the New Bottom Line, though this is deduced rather than stated.

military-superiority.rationale: Lerner replaces a Strategy of Domination with a Strategy of Generosity, so pursuing military superiority is rejected.

ethnic-nation.rationale: A nation defined by one ethnicity conflicts with the universal globalization of love and caring Lerner proposes, though he does not address it directly.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Lerner frames change as a transformation of values and consciousness rather than conflict, saying the goal is not to defeat the right but to build a better world.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Lerner's Global Marshall Plan transfers wealth to poor countries, but he frames it as generosity rather than reparations owed for colonialism.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Lerner names selfishness as the defect of the present system and replaces it with an ethic of caring and generosity.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The caring ethic stresses obligation to others, yet the movement is also rights-supporting, so sources give no ranking.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Lerner speaks of awe at the universe and ecological sanity, and says the ecological movement must be spiritual, implying nature's worth beyond use.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Lerner attacks consumerism and ecological damage but proposes rebuilding cities, not rejecting industrial society as a disaster.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Institutions judged by love and caring sit uneasily with algorithmic rule, but this is deduced from his institutional ethic.

restore-past-order.rationale: The movement seeks a transformed future society grounded in love and caring rather than restoring an earlier order.

direct-action.rationale: Sojourners and Tikkun use protest and lobbying alike, so neither is prioritized over elections.

means-match-ends.rationale: Lerner wants the anti-war movement to embody generosity and kindness, matching methods to the world he seeks.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Lerner wants eco-friendly cities and less consumption, not abandonment of civilization.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Lerner supports communal sharing of many produced goods and ending poverty, near a need-based principle.

production-for-use.rationale: The New Bottom Line asks that productivity be judged by love, social justice and ecological sanity rather than profit alone.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Lerner criticizes profit-maximization as a value but the sources do not adopt a theory of exploitation.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: A nonviolent, generosity-based movement is incompatible with class dictatorship.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Lerner links selfishness and domination to war but never claims inevitable imperial war from capitalism.

taxation-theft.rationale: Lerner objects to tax cuts for the rich and defends social programs funded by government.

conscription.rationale: Deduced from the peace commitments and opposition to the Iraq war.

exit-over-voice.rationale: A movement built on political participation and lobbying values voice, deduced rather than stated.

state-as-business.rationale: The New Bottom Line rejects running institutions by profit and efficiency measures.

media-academia-power.rationale: Sources focus on money and the religious right's power rather than universities and media, so this is deduced disagreement.

total-state.rationale: The movement seeks a loving society through voluntary moral transformation and persuasion, not state control of all life.

national-rebirth.rationale: Moral renewal is sought, but globally and without decadence rhetoric about the nation.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Expansion is the Strategy of Domination that Lerner explicitly rejects.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Feudal oath-based authority is absent from the sources and at odds with democratic values.

bound-labor.rationale: Serf-like obligations contradict the justice and dignity commitments, although never discussed.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Lerner supports a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine, which accepts Israel as a state.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Lerner discusses peace between the two sides but not a general right of return.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Lerner advocates economic democracy and a New Bottom Line applied to corporations.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Wallis calls budgets moral documents, implying spending on the poor should not yield to deficit rules.

force-without-un.rationale: Lerner demands an end to the Iraq war and opposes striking Iran, from which opposition to unilateral force follows.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Lerner criticizes progressives' hostility to spiritual consciousness and seeks awe and love alongside rationality.

class-collaboration.rationale: Lerner favors cooperation and kindness over conflict, but does not discuss employers and workers specifically.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Destroying inherited cultural institutions has no support in the sources.

dominated-front.rationale: A bloc against Western powers conflicts with the Strategy of Generosity, but is unmentioned.

workers-nation.rationale: Lerner's global solidarity conflicts with organizing by nation.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Wallis credits faith communities with driving the civil rights movement, whose aim was ending legal segregation.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Lerner treats government as a vehicle for loving legislation through covenant lobbying, not a pure class tool.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Lerner's ecological emphasis conflicts with expanding fossil fuel output, though energy policy is not specified.

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiracy theory with no place in the spiritual left.

national-mission.rationale: Wallis objects to the faith of Jesus being made pro-war and pro-American, rejecting national missions.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Lerner criticizes money in politics but does not call politicians corrupt as a class.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Lerner explicitly supports government health care, education and anti-poverty programs.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Lerner's ethic of love and caring for all, and a globalization of generosity, rests on the equal worth of every person.

socialism-one-country.rationale: An internal Marxist debate the spiritual left does not engage.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Lerner urges both Israelis and Palestinians to treat each other kindly rather than apply a colonial label.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Lerner opposes imposing a religion on everyone, which includes legally restricting free religious choice.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A socialist state doctrine outside the movement's concerns.

consent-of-governed.rationale: A movement relying on lobbying and democratic persuasion presupposes consent, but states no theory of legitimacy.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist export drives conflict with global solidarity, deduced.

population-transfer.rationale: Forced removal of a minority contradicts the kindness and mutual respect Lerner urges between peoples.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Lerner's New Bottom Line replaces selfishness and struggle with caring and cooperation as the basis of society.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Lerner's critique of the Strategy of Domination resonates with this view though he does not use the concept.

vanguard-party.rationale: Lerner builds change through broad spiritual and democratic persuasion, not a revolutionary elite.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Wallis argues poverty is a religious issue and that budgets neglecting the poor are unbiblical.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Lerner attributes poverty to selfishness and unequal distribution of resources, not population.

party-controls-media.rationale: State control of information contradicts the democratic, persuasion-based approach.

party-commands-army.rationale: Party control of the army belongs to one-party systems the movement does not hold.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Long waits conflict with a generous global ethic, deduced.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Lerner criticizes money in politics but nothing says representatives should earn only an average wage.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Executive concentration of power runs against the movement's anti-domination stance.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Church governance is outside the sources and varies by denomination.

clerical-rule.rationale: Lerner criticizes the religious right's political use of religion and opposes imposing a religion.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: The movement opposes the Iraq war but does not call for defeat of its own government.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: The sources oppose war but do not discuss permanent alliances or troop deployment.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: An extreme ownership mandate nobody in the sources proposes.

people-in-arms.rationale: An armed citizenry conflicts with the peace emphasis.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Lerner prefers ecologically rebuilt cities and does not exalt rural life.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Not a theme of the movement, which includes many clergy and academics.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Lerner's progressive religion rejects the religious right's use of scripture in policy.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Religious and liberal strands of the spiritual left disagree.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Exemptions pit religious liberty against equal law; the sources do not choose.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: An anti-colonial theme the sources do not engage.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Suspending freedoms for growth contradicts a values-first democratic movement.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Lerner's Global Marshall Plan has advanced countries dedicate 1-2% of GDP annually for twenty years to end poverty.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: The peace commitment points away from independent nuclear arsenals.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Lerner would want economic institutions answerable to a New Bottom Line beyond price stability, but central banks go unmentioned.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The New Bottom Line holds that economic activity should be judged by love, justice and ecological sanity rather than private gain alone.

collective-defense.rationale: The movement opposes wars like Iraq, but nothing in the sources addresses alliance guarantees.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Divine rulers embody domination and misuse of religion that Lerner condemns.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Lerner opposes tax cuts for the rich, implying support for progressive rates.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Classical constitutional theory is not engaged by the sources.

leader-cult.rationale: Mass leader worship is domination of a kind the movement rejects.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A Maoist debate the movement does not engage.

refugee-return.rationale: Lerner urges kindness between sides but takes no stand on return of refugees.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Claiming territory by nationality conflicts with the peace stance.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Lerner opposes imposing religion, including punishing departure from it.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: The movement's premise that ethical and spiritual change drives society opposes materialism.

moral-incentives.rationale: The New Bottom Line values love and generosity above the profit motive.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Armed vanguard action contradicts the nonviolent Strategy of Generosity.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Nation-centered history conflicts with the global ethos.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Paternal imperial rule is domination of the type Lerner rejects.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Lerner calls for transforming capitalism's bottom line but makes no claim about crisis or collapse.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Imperial legacy influence conflicts with anti-domination thinking.

delink-world-market.rationale: Global solidarity and the Marshall Plan favor integration with reform, not delinking.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist theory of imperialism that the sources do not use, though Lerner does favor transfers from rich to poor countries.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Wallis honors faith-led civil rights victories, which restricted private discrimination.

elective-rulers.rationale: A democratic movement favors election, deduced.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Parliamentary sovereignty versus monarchy is a British constitutional debate absent from the sources.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Wallis calls on the privileged to care for the poor but Lerner prefers structural change, so strands differ.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The network exists to bring spiritual values into politics through activism and covenant lobbying.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Lerner criticizes consumer culture but sources do not claim it pacifies.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Gramscian hegemony theory is not used by the sources, though Lerner does blame a culture of selfishness.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Lerner sees global inequality but does not state a dependency theory.

native-born-offices.rationale: Exclusion from office conflicts with equal-worth ethics.

party-own-road.rationale: An internal communist debate that the spiritual left does not engage.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: A Global Marshall Plan favors aid, so aid refusal is opposed.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Irredentism conflicts with the peace emphasis.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Military political guardianship contradicts a peace-first stance.

single-official-language.rationale: Restricting minority languages conflicts with pluralism.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Restricting foreign owners conflicts with global generosity but resonates with anti-corporate views; the sources do not decide.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Lerner urges people to consume less and rethink progress, treating consumerism as damaging.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Funding insurgents is a Strategy of Domination.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Troop interventions to enforce loyalty conflict with peace commitments.

corporate-influence.rationale: Lerner highlights money in politics as a core field of NSP work.

non-intervention.rationale: Pacifist-leaning but also sympathetic to humanitarian concerns.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Conspiracy against minorities contradicts equal worth.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Religious progressives generally value marriage as an institution.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Global cooperation points against national supremacy.

religious-nation.rationale: Lerner opposes imposing a religion on everyone.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Tribute and submission to a leading power is the hierarchy of domination Lerner proposes to replace with generosity.

defeat-communism.rationale: Cold-war confrontation is at odds with the peace emphasis.

religion-illusion.rationale: Lerner criticizes progressives' hostility to spiritual life ("religio-phobia") and insists the ecological movement must be spiritual.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Lerner endorses communal sharing but not a reorganization into small communes.

majority-settlement.rationale: State-encouraged settlement against minorities conflicts with justice commitments.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Lerner supports two states and mutual respect, not primacy of one claim.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Lerner opposes imposing a religion on everyone.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Exploitation of colonies is domination Lerner rejects.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Armed removal of rulers conflicts with peace commitments.

assisted-dying.rationale: Religious progressives are divided on assisted dying and the sources are silent.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Wallis claims to transcend left and right, but Lerner explicitly identifies as progressive.

alienated-labor.rationale: Lerner says modern workplaces push people to neglect meaning and love, which resembles alienation.

rich-first.rationale: Lerner's Marshall Plan demands solidarity rather than allowing some to prosper first.

property-franchise.rationale: Wealth qualification conflicts with equal worth.

reification.rationale: Marxist reification theory is not used by Lerner, even though his critique of treating people as means to profit is related.

racial-franchise.rationale: Wallis credits faith-driven civil rights and suffrage struggles.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Lerner's interfaith network and rejection of imposing a religion contradict legal bars on mixed-faith marriage.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Singling out a religious minority for avoidance contradicts the equal worth and interfaith respect the network stands on.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Lerner complains that progressives suffer from religio-phobia and hostility to spiritual consciousness, so state atheism would be anathema.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Lerner opposes cutting social programs and wants government action on poverty.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Drilled youth movements train for national service in a way that conflicts with the peace commitment.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The movement criticizes profit-first values but does not distinguish work income from property income.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Strands split between pacifists and just-war thinkers.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Academic feminist theory is not engaged by the sources.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Glorifying death for the nation sits badly with Lerner's rejection of militarism, though martyrdom language exists in religion.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Wikipedia defines the spiritual left as grounding politics in spiritual traditions, though not as a good-versus-evil struggle.

god-not-male.rationale: Progressive religion typically embraces inclusive God-language.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Reserving economic life for a majority group contradicts equal worth and the interfaith universalism of the network.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: A socialist definitional debate that the spiritual left does not enter.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Wikipedia defines the position as grounding left aims in spiritual traditions, and Lerner says institutions should serve love, awe and meaning.

dense-cities.rationale: Lerner favors rebuilt, eco-friendly cities that prioritize walking over cars.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The universalist ethic and Wallis's coalition approach cut against organizing by racial interest, though Wallis does prioritize racial justice.

communal-electorates.rationale: Separate electorates conflict with common community.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Paranoid nationalism is not part of the movement.

women-distinct-values.rationale: The movement stresses care and nonviolence, but the sources do not attribute them to women specifically.

arms-reduction.rationale: Lerner wants a peace movement and to redirect resources from the military to ending poverty.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: The Global Marshall Plan restructures world economic flows toward the poor.

smash-state-machine.rationale: The network works through lobbying legislators and a covenant, which assumes the existing state can be used.

sacred-nation.rationale: Sacralizing the nation conflicts with universal ethics.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Spiritual traditions affirm shared human nature.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Lerner's interfaith approach seeks common values but does not claim one truth.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Lerner opposes imposing one particular religion.

premarital-sex.rationale: Strands split between liberal and traditional religious.

women-suffrage.rationale: Wallis credits faith communities with women's suffrage.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Spiritual left defends religion's positive role.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Lerner criticizes the religious right's misuse of the Bible.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Defending bureaucratic planned economies is not part of the movement's concerns, which lean toward democratic reform.

national-church-status.rationale: Lerner opposes imposing one religion and the network is interfaith, so legal privilege for one church is opposed.

simple-living.rationale: Lerner urges consuming less and rethinking progress.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Killing suspected drug users without trial contradicts the love-and-caring ethic and basic justice.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Lerner supports universal health care and education.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: The network itself is an interest group that lobbies and organizes, so bypassing groups contradicts its method.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Interfaith respect and equal worth conflict with this.

women-must-cover.rationale: Coerced dress conflicts with the movement's commitments.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Interfaith respect rejects claims of incompatibility.

material-over-identity.rationale: Lerner's politics of meaning faults the left for focusing on material interests while ignoring spiritual and ethical needs; the New Bottom Line puts love and caring above material measures.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Lerner condemns cuts to social programs for the poor as a misuse of religion. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

former-empire-equal-treatment.rationale: Imperial legacy influence conflicts with anti-domination thinking. (Carried over from former-empire-influence, "A country should cultivate political and cultural influence in regions once ruled by its predecessor empire.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: Economic and public institutions should be judged by how much they promote love, caring and generosity, not only by profit and efficiency.
missingStatements.rationale: Lerner's New Bottom Line is the movement's central programmatic demand for economy, schools and government.

notes: Lerner (Jewish, explicitly progressive) and Wallis (evangelical, claims to transcend left and right) differ on abortion, same-sex marriage and church-state; those answers are held at neutral or low confidence. Most policy answers beyond economics, peace and ecology are inferences from the shared ethic.
